card.name: Theeyaattam
card.era: Traditional (documented continuously through 18th century to present)
card.tagline: A sacred Kerala ritual dance of powder artwork, drumbeats, and deity invocation.
card.profile: Theeyaattam, also known as Theeyaattu, is a traditional temple dance performance native to Kerala, India. It exists in two distinct lineages: Bhadrakali Theeyaattu, performed by the Theeyaattunni Brahmin community, and Ayyappan Theeyaattu, enacted by Thiyyadi Nambiars. The ritual combines elaborate ground paintings using colored powders, devotional singing, stylized storytelling dance, and trance-like oracle circumambulations. Staged in central and southern Kerala temples, the performance follows rigid sacred codes that remain strictly preserved.
card.insight: Before the dancer steps onto the floor, artists spend hours sketching the deity in five natural powders, only for the oracle to erase the sacred image under a frenzy of rhythmic coconut breaking.
card.profile_long:
Theeyaattam is an ancient ritualistic temple dance form rooted in the sacred traditions of Kerala. Divided strictly along hereditary community lines, Bhadrakali Theeyaattu is presented by the Theeyaattunni community in south-central Kerala districts such as Pathanamthitta, Alappuzha, Kottayam, and Ernakulam. Ayyappan Theeyaattu is preserved by the Thiyyadi Nambiar community across Thrissur, Palakkad, and Malappuram. Historical accounts trace the presence of Thiyyadi families in central Kerala to possible southward migrations from north Malabar during the 18th century.

A full performance of Ayyappan Theeyaattu traditionally unfolds across four interconnected phases: Kalamezhuthu, Kottum Pattum, Koothu, and Velichchappaadu. The ritual begins in daylight with Kalamezhuthu, the intricate drawing of the deity on a sanctified floor using five natural pigments. Once the sacred floor image is complete after approximately two hours, musicians initiate Kottum Pattum, singing invocatory Thottam verses accompanied by percussion instruments. The Koothu phase introduces dramatic gesture-laden dance storytelling without face makeup, leading into the climactic Velichchappaadu dance where an oracle circumambulates the sacred painting and erases it in a trance.

Music plays an integral role in driving the ritual's rhythm and sacred intensity. Vocal recitations blend archaic Malayalam and Tamil lyrics, incorporating melodic structures from Kerala's classical Sopanam tradition as well as Carnatic idioms. Rhythmic accompaniment is anchored by the chenda drum, the smaller para drum, and bronze ilathalam cymbals. In extended dawn-to-night Udayasthamaya performances, musicians and the oracle engage in Pantheeraayiram, an intense three- to four-hour physical ritual involving the rhythmic breaking of 12,000 coconuts to accelerating drum patterns.

The dancer's appearance varies significantly across the ritual phases and tradition variants. In Bhadrakali Theeyaattu, a male practitioner dresses as Goddess Bhadrakali, facing away from the sacred lamp to symbolize pockmarks from smallpox while recounting her victory over Darikasura. In Ayyappan Theeyaattu, the Koothu dancer wears defined traditional costumes without facial makeup, while the Velichchappaadu oracle appears bare-chested with a garland, flowing unknotted hair, and red and white cloth wrapped around the waist, wielding a small sword.

Theeyaattam serves as both an act of temple devotion and a solemn community offering. Sacred powder from the erased kalam is distributed to attendees as blessed prasadam, while the oracle utters revelatory kalpana trance pronouncements. Because of its deep ritual obligations and strict adherence to traditional codes, the art form resists modern commercial alterations and remains confined to sacred temple grounds and family shrines.
card.sacred_note: Theeyaattam is a sacred temple ritual governed by strict traditional codes. Outsiders must not disrupt the sacred floor painting (kalam), touch ritual items, or attempt to imitate the trance rituals outside proper temple contexts.

sections.origins_and_history: Theeyaattam developed as an hereditary temple art in Kerala, practiced exclusively by specialized temple-bound communities. Bhadrakali Theeyaattu belongs to the Theeyaattunni community in south-central Kerala, centered around temples such as Pallippurathu Kavu in Kottayam and Thrikkariyoor Mahadeva Temple. Ayyappan Theeyaattu is maintained by Thiyyadi Nambiars in central Kerala, whose ancestral lineage experts trace to 18th-century migrations from north Malabar. Revival and documentation efforts include publications by Mulankunnathukavu Thiyyaadi Raman Nambiar and work by the Shree Bhadra Kalasamajam in Kottayam.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance begins with minimal footwork during the dramatic Koothu phase, relying on hand gestures that resemble less refined forms of Koodiyattam and Kathakali with neutral facial expressions. During the Velichchappaadu phase, the oracle holds a small sword and initiates slow, measured steps while circumambulating the floor painting. Over 9 or 11 counter-clockwise circles, the movement tempo steadily accelerates until the oracle leaps onto the sacred powder image in a frenzy. The oracle then erases the body of the figure using both legs and clears the deity's face using the right hand.
sections.music_and_instruments: Music accompanies every phase following the floor painting. Songs blend old Malayalam and Tamil texts set to endemic Kerala tunes, classical Sopanam ragas, and Carnatic melodic structures. Primary instruments consist of the chenda drum, the smaller para drum, and ilathalam bronze cymbals. The rhythmic accompaniment ranges from steady invocatory beats to high-speed climactic patterns during the coconut-breaking Pantheeraayiram ritual.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performances occur on consecrated temple floors in front of a lighted nilavilakku brass lamp. In Bhadrakali performance, the male dancer adopts goddess attire and turns away from the lamp. In Ayyappan Koothu, dancers wear defined attire without facial paint. The Velichchappaadu oracle is bare-chested, wearing floral garlands, flowing hair, red and white waist drapes, and holding a small sword.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Bhadrakali Theeyaattu depicts the mythological victory of Goddess Bhadrakali over the demon Darikasura. Ayyappan Theeyaattu enacts the birth story of Lord Ayyappa, born of Shiva and Vishnu in Mohini form. The performance functions as an annual festival highlight or family offering, culminating in the distribution of kalam powder as divine prasadam and trance revelations called kalpana.
sections.notable_figures: Mulankunnathukavu Thiyyaadi Raman Nambiar is a prominent author and practitioner who documented the tradition in his book 'Ayyappan Theeyattu', written with support from V. R. Prabodhachandran Nayar.
sections.regional_variants: Bhadrakali Theeyaattu is concentrated in south-central Kerala (Pathanamthitta, Alappuzha, Kottayam, and Ernakulam districts). Ayyappan Theeyaattu is practiced in central Kerala (Thrissur, Palakkad, and Malappuram districts) with strong historical ties to Malabar.
sections.lineage: Bhadrakali Theeyaattu is inherited and transmitted through male members of the Theeyaattunni Brahmin community. Ayyappan Theeyaattu is inherited through male lineages of the Thiyyadi Nambiar ambalavasi community.

claims.text: Theeyaattam also known as Theeyaattu (Tīyāttu) is a traditional temple dance form of Kerala.
There are two types of Theeyaattam – Bhadrakali Theeyaattu and Ayyappan Theeyaattu.
Bhadrakali Theeyattu is performed by Theeyaattunnis whereas Ayyappan Theeyaattu is performed by Thiyyadi Nambiars.
The Bhadrakali Theeyattu dance depicts the war of goddess Bhadrakali with Darikasura where finally goddess Bhadrakali emerges as the winner.
The most common version of Thiyyattu involves four phases of presentation: Kalamezhuthu, Kottum Pattum, Koothu, and Velichchappaadu.
The oracle begins with slow steps while circumambulating around the kalam, but the tempo gains with the circles he make around 9 or 11 of them overall.
Theeyattu has strict traditional rituals which are strictly followed even now and cannot be modified at one's will.

episode_brief.title_hook: Powder, Drum, and Fire: The Sacred Erasing of Theeyaattam
episode_brief.logline: In the sacred temples of Kerala, hereditary artists spent hours painting a deity in colored powders, only to dance it into dust before midnight.
beats: Artists create the detailed deity kalam on the temple floor using five natural colored powders.
Musicians begin Kottum Pattum, filling the twilight with chenda drumbeats and archaic Sopanam chants.
The Koothu dancer enters, enacting sacred birth stories using classical hand gestures.
The oracle enters holding a small sword, walking 9 to 11 widening circles around the kalam as drums accelerate.
The oracle leaps into the sacred painting, erasing the powder deity in a rhythmic frenzy before distributing prasadam.
